# ds-workorder — Work Order Lifecycle

**Type:** Function-backed skill pack
**Invocation:** matched by per-mode triggers in `modes/*/metadata.yml`
**Not a CLI command.** The AI invokes one of the five modes below by calling the named function in `core.work_orders.*` and presenting the returned dict to the user.

The Dream Studio source-of-truth is the SQLite authority. This pack does not reason about work-order state from session memory or training knowledge. Every mode calls a named query or mutation function and surfaces its returned data.

---

## Mode dispatch

| Mode | File | Wraps | Keywords |
|------|------|-------|----------|
| start | `modes/start/SKILL.md` | `core.work_orders.start.start_work_order` | start work order:, begin work order: |
| execute | `modes/execute/SKILL.md` | `core.work_orders.mutations.mark_task_done` | mark task done:, task done:, complete task: |
| close | `modes/close/SKILL.md` | `core.work_orders.close.close_work_order` (+ `check_close_gates`) | close work order:, finish work order: |
| block | `modes/block/SKILL.md` | `core.work_orders.mutations.block_work_order` | block:, blocked by: |
| status | `modes/status/SKILL.md` | `core.work_orders.queries.list_work_orders` (+ `list_tasks`) | work order status:, show tasks: |

---

## Rules that apply to every mode

1. **Read functions before you write.** If a state-surfacing instruction below does not name the specific query function being called, stop and add it. Never narrate state from session context or training data.
2. **Present returned dicts. Don't invent fields.** The function returns a dict with a known shape. Show those fields. If the user asks for a field that isn't there, say so — don't fabricate it.
3. **Mutations require explicit user confirmation.** start, execute, close, block all mutate state. Confirm intent before calling the function, then call it, then show the user the returned dict so they can verify the change.
4. **Errors are operator-visible.** When a function returns `ok=False`, surface the `error` field verbatim. Do not paraphrase or soften the message.
5b. **An id you will USE comes from the CLI's output, never from your own rendering of it.** The CLI returns the complete 36-character key every time. If you print a shortened id in a survey, table, or diagnostic — `work_order_id[:8]` — that rendering is for the reader, and it is NOT a source you may type a command from. Copy the full id out of the CLI's own response.

   Observed twice in one session: an 8-character prefix was read back off a hand-written survey script and the remaining 28 characters were invented. `Task not found` both times, so nothing wrong was written — and only because the fabricated suffixes failed to collide. A guess that happens to hit a real id modifies the wrong record silently, and no gate downstream can catch it, because the write is well-formed.

   The temptation on hitting this is to add prefix resolution to the CLI. Do not: it puts a shortcut into a tool that already hands over the full key, and an ambiguous prefix then has to be either refused (no better than the current error) or guessed at (strictly worse). The defect is reading an id from the wrong place, not the length of the id.

5. **No raw UUIDs to the user unless asked.** Use the work_order_id internally; refer to the work order by its `title` in conversation. The user can ask for the ID.
6. **Task descriptions should include behavioral acceptance criteria.** When authoring tasks (via scope or during a WO), each task description should include an "Acceptance:" clause stating what the operator observes when the task is done. The independent review completion grader will emit a warning gap if feature/infrastructure WOs have no observable behavioral AC — this is not a fail, but it signals that the grader could not verify expected operator outcomes.

7. **SQL-CHECK lines for DB-state ACs.** A task's `acceptance_criteria` field may include one or more `SQL-CHECK:` lines (format: `SQL-CHECK: <SELECT statement>`). The completion grader executes these read-only against the authority DB before analyzing the diff. A query returning a non-zero/non-null first column passes; zero/null/no rows or any error fails. A `SQL-CHECK RESULT: FAIL` annotation forces that task to verdict `"missing"` regardless of diff evidence. Use SQL-CHECK when the task outcome is a database state change not visible in the diff (e.g. a migration row, a column added by bootstrap). See `docs/authoring/work-orders.md` for the full convention.

18. **A gate this engine cannot run REFUSES the close; it does not pass it.** A work order's gates are DATA — `business_work_order_types.pre_build_gate` and `post_build_gate`, each a `|`-separated list — so a gate name is whatever a row says it is. `run_gate_check` dispatches eleven names (`design_brief_locked`, `api_contract_exists`, `api_contract_and_security_review`, `spec_approved`, `all_tests_pass`, `design_critique`, `security_scan`, `game_validate`, `anti_slop_passed`, `independent_review`, `independent_review_passed`) and **refuses anything else**, naming the unknown gate and quoting the valid set back. It used to end in an unconditional pass, which made a gate nobody implemented byte-indistinguishable from a gate that ran and succeeded — so a typo in a type row, a rename applied on one side only, or an external project's aspirational gate name all closed the work order clean and said nothing. Declaring NO gate is still fine and still passes: absence is a choice, an unrunnable name is not. If you hit this, correct the name on the work order type or implement the gate; `--force` gets past it and is recorded as a `gate.bypassed` event, which is the point of reaching for it deliberately rather than by accident.

8. **Executable acceptance criteria BLOCK close (always-on AC gate).** `close_work_order` runs every task's `acceptance_criteria` as executable checks and blocks close on any failure, regardless of WO type. Three line-prefixes are supported: `SQL-CHECK: <SELECT>` (read-only DB query, passes on truthy first column), `TEST-CHECK: <pytest-node-id>` (runs that pytest node in a subprocess; passes iff exit 0), and `API-CHECK: <METHOD path -> [status]>` (boots the API via TestClient; passes on 2xx/expected status + non-empty body). A WO **cannot close without `force=True` unless it has at least one executable check** across its tasks — author at least one SQL/TEST/API-CHECK AC per WO. `force=True` bypasses and emits `gate.bypassed`. The legacy `all_tests_pass` gate now executes the WO's TEST-CHECKs instead of grepping `test-results.md`.

9. **Every task must be done before close (tasks_done gate).** `close_work_order` blocks the close when any task is not `complete` (or deliberately `cancelled`) — no 0/N or partial closes ("NOTHING LEFT HANGING"). Mark each task via the execute mode (`mark_task_done`) before closing; `force=True` bypasses and records a `gate.bypassed` event carrying the `tasks_done` reason. Both the CLI close path and the autonomous execute-work-orders loop go through the same `close_work_order`, so enforcement is identical everywhere. Close also runs a projection tick before reading task statuses, so a freshly marked-done task is never misread as still-pending.

10. **Escalation ladder (escalated WOs).** When the deterministic verifier/outcome-eval says a closed WO is NOT FIXED, the platform reopens it and escalates (`core/work_orders/escalation.py`, table `ds_escalations`): (a) the retry is routed to a more capable model — `resolve_executor` returns `opus` for an escalated WO; both the autonomous loop (the `escalation-probe` node + `ds work-order executor <id>`) and the manual path (`start_work_order`'s `executor` field) honor it. (b) Re-close REQUIRES a *passing* independent review — for an escalated WO the `independent_review` gate cannot be bypassed by unreviewable/gap shortcuts OR by `force=True` (`close_work_order` returns `escalated: True` and refuses). (c) Retries are capped (`escalation.retry_cap`, env `DREAM_STUDIO_ESCALATION_RETRY_CAP` > `ds_config` > default 3); at the cap the ladder stops auto-reopening and writes an `ESC-RETRYCAP-*` operator escalation — no silent loop.

11. **Attribution guard — fit-check before you file; do NOT auto-attribute to the active milestone/WO.** When new work surfaces (the operator pivots mid-work-order, or a work order / task is being created), never default it into the currently-active milestone or work order just because it is active. First fit-check the proposed work against the open milestones' described scope — run `ds project fit-check --title "<title>" --description "<description>"` (a read-only wrapper over `core.projects.queries.fit_check_work_order(...)`) and read the `verdict`:
    - `clear_single` — exactly one milestone clearly fits; bind it there.
    - `ambiguous` / `no_fit` / `no_milestones` — **STOP AND ASK** the operator which milestone this belongs to (offer a different existing milestone, or a new milestone / separate project). Do not guess, and do not fall back to the active/most-recent milestone.
    Both the milestone and the work order describe the work they contain; compare the proposed work to those descriptions before binding anything. Filing separate engagements into one active milestone is the mis-attribution this guard prevents — asking is cheaper than the re-work it causes.

12. **Verify graders and live evals spawn through a provider-neutral runner.** The close/verify path's independent-review graders and the live evals do NOT hardcode a vendor CLI — they spawn through `core.adapters.grader_runner`, which resolves the provider from a per-role *profile* (`config.grader_profiles.resolve_grader_profile`). Which provider grades a role is selected by this precedence (highest first): `DS_GRADER_STUB` (a stub-script path — headless/CI) → the `--grader-profile` CLI flag → the per-role env `DS_GRADER_PROFILE_<ROLE>` → a `DS_GRADER_PROFILE_CONFIG` file → the built-in registry default (the vendor CLI). Inspect the resolved role→provider mapping before verifying with `ds grader profiles`. A provider that is not invocable degrades that grader to `unreviewable` (surfaced in the verdict, never a false-done); it does not crash verify. Any provider whose output validates against the published grader-verdict contract (`schemas/grader_verdict*.schema.json`) can back the graders — that is what makes the verification plane portable.

13. **Two structural invariants block close, and they judge only work orders the AUTHORITY created.** A work order carries at least 2 tasks; its milestone carries at least 2 work orders. Both are checked at CLOSE, not at creation or start — a work order has zero tasks when created and often still has zero when started (ds-project decomposes only the first work order of the first milestone), so start REPORTS and close REFUSES. The escape is a recorded reason, `ds work-order close <id> --accept-structure "<why>"`, stored as an `operator_decision` artifact; `--force` is the wrong tool because it bypasses every gate at once and records no reasoning about this one. **Scope:** only a work order carrying a `work_order.created` event is judged — that is what distinguishes one the authority authored from a row inserted directly, and it is why hermetic test fixtures are exempt. A gate that cannot READ its data blocks (an unevaluated verdict is not a clean one); a database with no canonical event table is simply not judged, because it is not an authority.

14. **A verdict is scoped to the commits the work order owns, and says when it is not.** A delivery boundary is a contiguous commit RANGE, so several work orders landing on one branch share a span — and verify used to grade one work order against all of them. Measured on WO 1db6de49: 10 commits from 5 work orders, six review rounds attaching ~30 tasks each while every round confirmed its own work had landed. `core/work_orders/range_attribution.py` now records which commits a work order owns (at each `mark_task_done` and at close) and verify grades only those. **Read the attribution note on the verdict.** A range predating the recording, or one where no neighbour claimed anything, is graded at FULL WIDTH and says so — treat findings there as possibly belonging to a branch neighbour, and prefer carrying them (`ds work-order carry-over`) over absorbing them. Overlapping boundaries alone never narrow a range: interleaved work orders have overlapping time windows, and subtracting on them drops commits that genuinely belong.
15. **A task nobody can check cannot be filed (admission at intake).** `ds work-order add-task` and the review fan-out both run `core/work_orders/admission.py` BEFORE the task is created. **So does `create_task` itself** — the mutation runs the Warden's lane on its own, because that is the door this pack and every skill, workflow and hook is told to import directly, and a guard on one of two writers holds only for whichever writer the author reached for. Measured: 43% of the tasks created in the month AFTER the CLI door was guarded still arrived with no criterion. Only the Warden runs in the mutation (whether a criterion exists and can be run is a property of the text); the Surveyor and Herald need a database, sibling titles and the repo, so the full round table stays at the CLI. The predicate is IMPORTED by both, never restated. **`why=` is accepted by the mutation and composed into the description there**, so a skill calling it directly gets the marker the ratchet reads rather than a bare bypass. **One exemption, and it is a move rather than an authoring:** `carried_from=<task_id>` skips the floor for `carry_over`, which re-files an EXISTING task under a new work order — refusing there would delete a task already in the authority, not raise the standard. It takes a task id, not a boolean, so it cannot be set by an author who simply wants past the floor. Three seats decide: **the Warden** requires an executable criterion (`TEST-CHECK:` / `SQL-CHECK:` / `API-CHECK:`) or a declared reason of 20+ characters via `--why "<reason>"`; **the Surveyor** refuses a task whose named files fall outside the work order's `Module boundary:` clause, and reports UNKNOWN when no boundary is declared rather than admitting by default; **the Herald** refuses a duplicate title, and REPORTS — without refusing — a task whose acceptance criterion an open sibling on the same work order already carries. Every refusal names the seat and the remedy, and exits 1 — a refusal that exited 0 would be a suggestion. **The shared-criterion finding is an observation, not a refusal, and the distinction is deliberate.** Two open tasks under one TEST-CHECK are satisfied by a single run, so the second cannot fail independently — which is a defect when the later task is the earlier one reworded, and correct when one check genuinely covers two changes (measured: WO 20796691 carries a docstring edit and the assertion that reads it under one node that passes only when both are done). Nothing at intake can tell those apart, so `add-task` prints `NOTED (a-finding-already-filed): ...` and files the task; confirm the check covers both, or give the new task a criterion that distinguishes it. **The observation NAMES the open task that already holds the criterion**, and the unknown carries it as `holder` -- being told a duplicate exists with nowhere to look costs attention and buys nothing. Measured on the live authority when this landed: 4 groups covering 9 open tasks shared a criterion, and in all 35 same-gap-key duplicate groups the TITLES differed — so title dedup caught none of them. **`--why` is a DECLARATION, not a flag:** the reason is persisted into the task description, so a close later rests visibly on someone reading rather than on computation. **What this replaced:** the command used to create the task and then print "No executable acceptance criterion. Close cannot verify this task without one" — the consequence named exactly, enforced by nothing. Measured before this landed: **1766 of 3278 tasks (53%) carried no criterion**, and `_attach_gap_tasks` hardcoded `acceptance_criteria: None`. A refused finding is **reported, never dropped** — it arrives on the verdict under `unfiled_findings` with the seat and reason, because a finding discarded for lacking a criterion is invisible, which is worse than the stub it replaced. The blocking gate `task-criteria-baseline` holds the count at its recorded ceiling; raising it is a reviewable act (`--update`). **When the Surveyor refuses a task that genuinely belongs to the work order, the boundary is what is wrong — correct it, do not vague the task.** `ds work-order amend-boundary <id> --module-boundary '<paths>' --reason '<30+ chars>'` records the prior clause and why it moved, mirroring `repoint-ac`. The new boundary is VALIDATED: every path must exist, because otherwise widening scope until a refused task is admitted would be one command away. This matters because attribution judges only paths a description NAMES, so the cheapest way past a correct refusal is a vaguer description — which trades an honest refusal for a silent misattribution.
17. **The context artifact carries the PROMPT CHAIN, and it is the first thing to read.** `ds work-order start` writes a context artifact that now opens with `## The prompt chain`: why the project exists, what the milestone delivers, and what this work order is for, top-down and placed BEFORE the gates — the first question an executor needs answered is what the work is for, not which gates will judge it. Each pending task's acceptance criterion is rendered under its own task, because the criterion is the half that decides whether the task is done and the title alone is the name of the work without the definition of finished. **This is new as of 2026-09-22 and the absence it replaced was total:** `read_work_order_brief` ran four queries against four tables and selected four titles — `business_projects.name`, `business_milestones.title`, `business_work_orders.title`, `business_tasks.title` — and not one description, so a work order arrived as a name with a list of task names under it and the executor had to infer the goal from the diff. A layer carrying no prompt prints no heading, so an absent section means the record predates the floors, not that there is nothing to know.

16. **`task-done` can FAIL, and a failed one means the task is not done.** `mark_task_done` reports the status the authority HOLDS — it reads `business_tasks` back after writing rather than asserting `"complete"`. This exists because a projection failure does not raise: `framework_engine_dispatch` catches a handler error, dead-letters the event, and returns normally, so the old contract reported `"complete"` for a task whose row was never written (measured: event `d441e451` reached the canonical log, failed a FOREIGN KEY constraint in the projection, and task `c1698f88` has no `business_tasks` row to this day while its caller was told the task was complete — and the `tasks_done` close gate counts exactly the rows that were never written). **Two outcomes that look identical in the read model are deliberately kept apart.** A completion whose event is durable but not yet materialized is `ok: True` with `read_model_pending` — say so instead of reporting a clean finish, and expect `ds work-order tasks` to lag until the next pass. A completion whose event the projection QUEUED or DEAD-LETTERED is `ok: False`: it will not recover unaided, the error names `ds projection dead-letter list`, and you must **not** mark the todo complete or move to the next task. `all_tasks_complete` and the delivery-boundary stamp are gated on the same verdict, so a lost completion no longer chains into close.
